entries.topic: From nationalization to the decision for war, July–October 1956: the crisis diplomacy and Israel's stated case

claims.text: Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company on 26 July 1956, after the United States and Britain refused to provide economic aid to Egypt; Eden's private judgment, as Hahn quotes it, was that "the Egyptian has his thumb on our windpipe." (Nationalization itself is told in Stage Two; this is the hinge only.)
The Company was a joint British-French enterprise that had run the Canal since its construction in 1869; Nasser offered "full economic compensation for the Company."

On 9 September 1956 Dulles proposed a Suez Canal Users' Association of "18 of the world's leading maritime nations"; the Office of the Historian records that it failed to win full support from any of the contending powers, and that through August–October Britain "repeatedly hinted that it might resort to force."

FRUS vol. XVI organizes the pre-war weeks under these headings, which name the parallel crises: the London conferences and SCUA (August–September); "Increasing Violence Along the Israel–Jordan Border" and the Macmillan visit (19 September–4 October); and, for 5–29 October, the Security Council debate, "the Iraqi Proposal to Move Troops Into Jordan", Anglo-American differences over SCUA and "Israeli Mobilization".

On 15 October 1956, two weeks before the war, Ben-Gurion told the Knesset (169th session) that 5716 had been "a turning point in our security situation", said Egypt "still sits in the Gaza Strip", and stated that between 1954 and 1955 Egypt had caused Israel 242 casualties; he presented the government's posture as defensive preparation rather than a first strike.

The Jewish Agency's historical account states that between 1948 and 1956 "a total of 1,300 Israeli citizens were killed or wounded" in cross-border attacks, records Egypt's announcement in September 1955 closing the Straits of Tiran to all vessels, and the Egypt–Syria military treaty of October 1955 that Jordan later joined. These are the figures Israel's case rests on; they are the Agency's, not an independent tally.

In his 7 November 1956 Knesset speech Ben-Gurion gave the reasons for the war as the renewed fedayeen raids, "the maritime blockade of Israel and the organization of an economic blockade against Israel throughout the world", the Czechoslovak arms ("enormous quantities of heavy arms"), and a "tripartite military alliance" of Egypt, Jordan and Syria with forces "placed under Egyptian command".

According to the Gush Katif Heritage Center's history (citing Hagai Huberman), on 29 March 1955 Ben-Gurion, then defence minister, proposed reconquering the Gaza Strip and the government rejected it; at the October 1956 cabinet meeting approving the operation he listed among the war's aims "[control of] the Gaza Strip."
Ben-Gurion described the campaign afterwards as "an action in self-defence in accordance with Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations."

disputes.question: Was Israel's war of October 1956 a war of self-defence or a war of choice?

positions.view: Israel's case: two years of fedayeen raids organized from Gaza, the Tiran and Canal blockades, the Czech arms flow and the new joint Arab command made a pre-emptive campaign self-defence under Article 51 (Ben-Gurion, 15 October and 7 November 1956; 5 March 1957; the Jewish Agency's casualty figures).

The critical case: the timing and form of the attack were set by a secret plan with Britain and France to give them a pretext to seize the Canal, and Ben-Gurion's own aims at Sèvres reached to territory (Shlaim: 'a monument to French opportunism, Eden's duplicity, and Ben-Gurion's paranoia'); Gaza was listed as a war aim at the approving cabinet meeting.

entries.topic: The Sèvres conference and protocol, 14–25 October 1956: who met, what was signed, and how it was hidden

claims.text: On 14 October 1956 at Chequers, General Maurice Challe, with acting foreign minister Albert Gazier, put to Eden the 'Challe scenario': Israel would attack Egypt in Sinai, giving Britain and France a pretext to occupy the Canal Zone. Shlaim quotes Nutting that Eden "could scarcely contain his glee" and Eden's reply, "So that lets us off the hook."

The conference opened at a villa in Sèvres at 4 p.m. on Monday 22 October: Selwyn Lloyd (incognito, with Donald Logan) for Britain; Ben-Gurion, Dayan and Peres for Israel (Mordechai Bar-On as secretary); Mollet, Pineau, Bourgès-Maunoury, Challe, Mangin and Abel Thomas for France. The British were absent on 23 October; Patrick Dean and Logan arrived at 4:30 p.m. on 24 October and the protocol was signed that evening.

The protocol has seven articles (paraphrased from Shlaim): (1) Israel launches a large-scale attack on the evening of 29 October aiming to reach the Canal Zone the next day; (2) on 30 October Britain and France appeal to both sides to stop and withdraw ten miles from the Canal, Egypt also to accept Anglo-French occupation of key positions, with twelve hours to reply; (3) if Egypt refuses, Anglo-French forces attack early on 31 October; (4) Israel will occupy the western shore of the Gulf of Aqaba and the islands of Tiran and Sanafir, which Britain and France neither support nor oppose; (5) Israel will not attack Jordan, and Britain will not aid Jordan if Jordan attacks Israel; (6) strict secrecy; (7) entry into force on the three governments' agreement.

Dayan's revised plan called for "a real act of war": a paratroop drop on the Mitla Pass, about thirty miles from the Canal, with a mechanized brigade's thrust westward, so that Britain would have a credible pretext to intervene about 36 hours later.

On 22 October Ben-Gurion laid out a reorganization of the region he himself called "fantastic": dividing Jordan, extending Israel to the Litani, internationalizing the Canal, with Nasser removed. An Israeli eighth point, added at his request, sought "permanent annexation of the entire area east of the El Arish-Abu Ageila, Nakhl-Sharm el-Sheikh" line; Pineau recorded it, but Britain and France never backed it and it is not in the signed text. On 24 October he said: "The Straits of Tiran are the State of Israel's Suez Canal."

Ben-Gurion feared Egyptian bombing ("Tel Aviv could be wiped out") unless the RAF first destroyed Egypt's air force, and feared British betrayal; Shlaim records that he took the initiative in proposing a written protocol as "a guarantee against betrayal by Perfidious Albion."

The protocol was signed by Patrick Dean (ad referendum), Christian Pineau and David Ben-Gurion. Eden "was clearly surprised and very put out" that it had been committed to paper and ordered all copies "rounded up and delivered to No. 10 for destruction"; the British copy was destroyed, and Dean and Logan's attempt on 25 October to get the French and Israelis to destroy theirs failed.

Ben-Gurion's copy, 'thrust deep into the pocket of his waistcoat', was kept in the Ben-Gurion Archives and became public after photocopying was permitted for a BBC documentary in 1996; a contemporary account of that search says the British copy was reportedly "burned almost as soon as it was signed" and the French said theirs had been "misplaced". A photocopy of the three French pages was found by Pineau's widow in 2002 (Wikipedia, reference only).

Peres wrote that during a break before the signing on 24 October he "finalized with these two leaders [Mollet and Bourgès-Maunoury] an agreement for the building of a nuclear reactor at Dimona"; an earlier reactor agreement dated from 21 September 1956; Pineau opposed and Mollet was undecided; in September 1957 France delivered a reactor of twice the previously promised capacity. The Dimona story itself belongs to Stage Four.
Eden denied for the rest of his life that there had been any collusion with Israel. US officials, Hahn writes, did not anticipate the collusion before hostilities began.
Shlaim's verdict: "The Protocol of Sèvres was thus a monument to French opportunism, Eden's duplicity, and Ben-Gurion's paranoia." (Interpretation.)

disputes.question: Who drove the plot, and was Israel's part a choice or a necessity?

positions.view: Shlaim: France was the matchmaker, Eden duplicitous, and Ben-Gurion's demand for a written guarantee came from a mistrust of Britain verging on paranoia; Israel's wider aims (the 'fantastic' plan, the annexation point) show more than self-defence.

Israel's own account frames its part as self-defence against Egypt's raids and blockade, with France as the only arms supplier willing to help; Oren argues the war partly completed what the 1949 armistices left open.

claims.text: The IDF dates the start of Operation Kadesh to 17:00 on 29 October 1956, with the first paratroop landing in Israel's military history near the eastern approaches of the Mitla Pass, and says the campaign lasted 100 hours under Lt. Gen. Moshe Dayan. (Oren writes that the landing came 'at dawn'; the IDF time is used here.)
The IDF Archives state that IDF forces occupied the peninsula 'within 100 hours' and that the war began on 29 October and the peninsula was occupied by 5 November 1956.
Israel occupied the Gaza Strip on 2 November and Sharm el-Sheikh on 5 November 1956 (dates per Wikipedia's year chronology and Morris's account of the occupation beginning 2–3 November).

Egyptian forces resisted at Abu Uwayqilah (Abu Ageila) and the Mitla Pass; after the Anglo-French bombing of the air bases Nasser pulled troops out of Sinai to protect the Canal; Nasser later claimed Egypt "had not been defeated by the Israelis" but had withdrawn to defend the Canal.

Keightley's despatch: RAF Valiant and Canberra bombers began attacking Egyptian airfields at 16:15 GMT on 31 October; by the end of 2 November the Egyptian Air Force was 'all but' neutralized; about 600 men of 3 Parachute Battalion Group jumped onto Gamil airfield at 08:20 GMT on 5 November with about 460 French paratroopers at Port Fuad; Royal Marine commandos landed at 04:50 GMT on 6 November, 45 Commando by 22 helicopters.

The cease-fire, ordered from London at 17:00 GMT on 6 November, took effect at 23:59 GMT; the Anglo-French force ashore peaked on 1 December at 13,500 British and 8,500 French troops; the last troops were aboard by 17:10 GMT on 22 December 1956.

Israeli dead, competing figures: 171 soldiers killed in battle (IDF site); 172 IDF soldiers (Jewish Agency); 'about 150 killed' (Ben-Gurion, 7 November 1956, an early count); '170 killed and 1 prisoner' (Ben-Gurion, 5 March 1957); 189 killed and 899 wounded (Janda, EBSCO). The official later figures cluster at 170–172.

Egyptian losses, competing estimates: about 1,650 ground forces killed, about 4,900 wounded and more than 6,000 captured or missing 'per foreign military observers' (Library of Congress country study); an estimated 1,030 killed and 4,000 wounded (Janda); 'well in excess of 1,000 military killed' (naval-history.net's estimate, since Keightley called Egyptian losses 'much more difficult to assess'). No Egyptian official total was found.

Port Said and Port Fuad: the British estimated 650 Egyptians died in Port Said during the invasion and occupation and 100 more in Port Fuad (Weeks's summary, which leaves unclear what share were civilians); Keightley's despatch records 'some 60 of the enemy' killed at Port Fuad. Egypt's UN letter of 5 November 1956 (A/3292) alleged attacks on civilians but gave no figures. The Port Said civilian toll is not settled by these sources.

British and French dead: Keightley's despatch gives 16 British killed and 96 wounded, and 10 French killed and 33 wounded; on 12 December 1956 the Defence Ministry told the Commons the latest figure was 21 British killed and 112 wounded (the later figure includes deaths during the occupation, such as the officer killed in a December ambush).

On 27 December 1956, 5,580 Egyptian prisoners of war were exchanged for four Israelis held by Egypt (South African History Online). Janda gives the forces as 45,000 Israelis against 30,000 Egyptians; Ben-Gurion told the Knesset Egypt had 'over 30,000 men' in Sinai.

At a debriefing of the senior command on 27 December 1956 Ben-Gurion warned against learning the wrong lesson: "this was a war deluxe", "You cannot learn from it how to fight the next war", and there was "no basis to assume that in the next war, we will have helping forces from abroad."

disputes.question: How many died in the 1956 war?

positions.view: Israeli official figures: 170–172 Israeli dead (IDF 171; Jewish Agency 172; Ben-Gurion 170 plus one prisoner); a reference work gives 189.

Egyptian losses rest on foreign estimates only: about 1,650 (US Library of Congress, citing observers), about 1,030 (Janda), 'well over 1,000' (naval-history.net); Port Said's dead are a British estimate of 650 plus 100 at Port Fuad, with the civilian share unclear.

disputes.question: Did Egypt lose the Sinai battle or withdraw from it?

positions.view: Israel's account: the IDF 'crushed' the Egyptian army and took the peninsula in 100 hours.

Nasser's account: Egypt withdrew from Sinai to defend the Canal against the Anglo-French attack and was not defeated by Israel; the Library of Congress study records real resistance at Abu Ageila and the Mitla Pass before the pull-back.

claims.text: On 29 October 1956, the first day of the war, Arab villages in Israel near the Jordanian line (the 'Little Triangle', ceded by Jordan under the 1949 armistice) were placed under a wartime curfew from 5 p.m. to 6 a.m.; Palestinian citizens then numbered about 160,000 and lived under military government (PalQuest; the regime itself is told in rd6).

The Jewish Virtual Library account says the order was given to the Border Police at 3:30 p.m., before most villagers could be told, and that 'any Arab on the streets was to be shot'; PalQuest and Wikipedia record that a sergeant told Kafr Qasim's mukhtar at 4:30 p.m. that the curfew would begin at 5 p.m.; Robinson describes a curfew announced only thirty minutes before.

Colonel Issachar Shadmi, the brigade commander, changed the curfew hours; Major Shmuel Malinki testified that Shadmi said 'I don't want sentimentality and I don't want arrests', and Malinki relayed to his men: 'Anyone leaving his home shall be shot; there shall be no arrests.' Shadmi denied that the question of villagers returning from work came up. (Testimony as summarized in Wikipedia's account of the trial record.)

The mukhtar asked about some 400 villagers still in the fields and was told they would be taken care of. Between 5 and 6:30 p.m., in nine shooting incidents at the village's western entrance, Lt. Gabriel Dahan's platoon shot workers returning on foot, by bicycle and by truck.

The count, with every competing figure: 47 (Jewish Virtual Library; Encyclopaedia Judaica; Jonathan Cook's 2008 article; JTA in 2016); 48 (JTA in November 1957, 'the murder of 48 Arabs'; Robinson, 'the border-patrol killing of 48 Palestinian citizens'; Times of Israel 2021, with an unborn child as a 49th); 49 (Kafr Qasim's own commemoration, JTA in 1999, Ynet 2014, the Knesset highlights page, President Herzog in 2021); 'fifty' (Middle East Eye). The difference lies mainly in whether the unborn child of a pregnant victim is counted and in sources' rounding; the breakdown most often given is 19 men, 6 women and 23 children aged 8–17.
Ynet (2014) adds that 13 people were wounded.

No villagers were shot in the other villages under Shadmi's command because local commanders did not carry out the order as Malinki's unit did; the scene record says two of the three units given the order disregarded it.

News of the killings was censored and the public learned of them weeks later (Jewish Virtual Library). An internal inquiry began on 1 November; Communist MKs Tawfik Toubi and Meir Vilner entered the village about two weeks later; Ben-Gurion first referred to the incident publicly on 12 November, and it took about two months of lobbying before the media blackout was lifted (Wikipedia). Cook reports Ben-Gurion's remark: 'those who gave the order will get a strict verdict. I don't think the soldiers are guilty.'

PalQuest records that journalists, activists and Communist Knesset members reached the village despite checkpoints, and that the government and army used 'a variety of tactics' to conceal the killings.

disputes.question: How many were killed at Kafr Qasim?

positions.view: 47 or 48: the Encyclopaedia Judaica and Jewish Virtual Library (47), the 1957 JTA dispatch and Shira Robinson (48).
49: the village's own commemoration and most later Israeli reporting (Ynet, Times of Israel, President Herzog), counting the unborn child of a pregnant victim; one outlet says fifty.

claims.text: Eleven Border Police officers and men were charged (JVL; Ynet says 13 were tried) before a military court presided over by Judge Benjamin Halevy, in case MD/57/3, the Military Advocate v. Major Shmuel Malinki and 10 others; the footnoted protocol sessions run from March 1957 to January 1958 (Orbach).

The verdict, 16 October 1958 (reported by JTA from Tel Aviv on 24 October): Major Shmuel Malinki 17 years; Lt. Gabriel Dahan and Lance Cpl. Shalom Offer 15 years each; Corporals Gavriel Ulliel and Edmond Nachmani and Privates Makhluf Karoush, Eliyahu Avraham and Albert Pahims seven years each; officers were stripped of rank. Eight were convicted.

The court held that an officer 'should display courage not only in the face of the enemy', stated its 'clear and unreserved belief' that it is forbidden for a soldier in any army to 'kill without due process of law', and found that Malinki had extended the illegal order 'by including women and children'.

Halevy's test of manifest illegality, as quoted by Leora Bilsky: 'Illegality that pierces the eye and revolts the heart' overrides the duty to obey; the ruling is the origin of the 'black flag' doctrine on manifestly unlawful orders still taught in the IDF. Orbach argues the doctrine emerged from the clash between the trial's attorneys, defendants and judges, not from the bench alone, and that the trial reshaped civil–military relations and the civic status of the Arab minority.

Reactions in October 1958: the defendants' families campaigned for pardons; Chief of Staff Chaim Laskov told the chief military prosecutor to study whether further trials, including of Shadmi, were needed; Herut said the verdict had 'left confusion in the minds of soldiers'; elders in Kafr Qasim called it 'courageous' and 'just'; the Jordanian paper Falastin praised its 'firmness' but alleged Shadmi had been smuggled abroad.

Shadmi was tried separately by a special court-martial; Orbach notes the prosecutor, Brig. Gen. Moshe David, did not hold him responsible for the killings and charged only procedural offences. In February 1959 he was acquitted of murder and convicted of extending the curfew without authority.

Shadmi's fine, as variously stated: '10 prutot' (Wikipedia, '+972', Hyehudi/Segev); 10 prutot described as '1/1000 of an old Israeli pound' (JVL, an internal inconsistency, since 10 prutot was 1/100); 'a single pruta (a thousandth of the Israeli pound)' (PalQuest); 'one-hundredth of an Israeli lira' (the simulation's mg_s01); 'a penny' (Cook). Ten prutot, one hundredth of a lira, is the figure most sources share.

Reductions: the appeal court (3 April 1959) cut Malinki to 14 years and Dahan to 10; the Chief of Staff to 10 and 8; President Ben-Zvi pardoned or reduced others; with a one-third remission all were out of prison by about November 1959 (Wikipedia); 'no one served more than three and a half years' (JVL); 'by 1960, all soldiers had been released' (PalQuest).

After release, Malinki was put in charge of security at the Negev Nuclear Research Center and Dahan was placed in charge of 'Arab affairs' in Ramla in 1960 (Wikipedia); PalQuest says the government 'compensated' the killers with official posts, including over Arab citizens in Lydda.

Yeshayahu Leibowitz responded in Haaretz (quoted in Tom Segev's The Seventh Million) with a sarcastic call for 'a mass petition' to revise the Nuremberg judgments, since the convicted men had also acted on orders.

disputes.question: Was the trial accountability or its absence?

positions.view: A landmark: Israel's own military court convicted its soldiers of murder and created the manifestly-unlawful-order doctrine (Orbach; Rivlin and Herzog later).

Its limits: the commander who set the order was fined a token sum, all sentences were cut to under four years, and two convicted officers were given posts in security and Arab affairs (PalQuest calls it 'a mockery of justice').

claims.text: A special commission recommended IL5,000 to the heirs of each man and woman killed, other sums for dependants and the wounded, and an extra IL1,000 for the heirs of a pregnant woman; Ben-Gurion pledged to honour it (JTA, Jerusalem, November 1957). The Encyclopaedia Judaica says a public board under Petah Tikva's mayor Pinhas Rashish decided to pay IL500,000 in all. Cook reports that one survivor, Saleh Khalil Issa, received 700 lira, less than a year's wage.

On 20 November 1957, over 400 guests, including cabinet ministers, Mapai legislators, military-government officials and Histadrut leaders, attended a state-organized 'ceremony of reconciliation' called a sulha, publicized in state-sponsored Arabic and Hebrew press (Robinson).

Robinson calls it a 'charade' villagers were pressured to attend; Slyomovics and Khleif describe it as 'forced upon the villagers' (as cited by Wikipedia); PalQuest says the villagers did prevent the accused from being brought to it.

The first monument (1976) called the killings a 'painful tragedy' without naming the perpetrators; a museum opened on 29 October 2006, when Education Minister Yuli Tamir also ordered schools to commemorate the event.

Plan Mole (Hafarperet): transcripts released in 2022 contain the testimony of Border Police commander Chaim Levy that Shadmi had said 'it's desirable that there be some fatalities' and that 'the killing of a few people as an intimidation measure can encourage movement eastward', with references to a plan to move the Triangle's Arab population to Jordan in wartime (Haaretz's reporting of 29 July 2022 as summarized by Peoples Dispatch and Middle East Eye). Tom Segev had earlier written that the sealing-off of the villages was part of 'a contingency plan to expel the inhabitants to Jordan under cover of the war' (quoted by Cook, 2008).

The text of Plan Mole and related military documents remained redacted after the 2022 release (PalQuest; The New Arab says 'information on an Israeli plan to deport' Palestinian citizens to Jordan was withheld). What the plan ordered, and whether the killing was meant to trigger it, therefore rests on testimony, not on the plan's own text.

The declassification: historian Adam Raz of the Akevot Institute applied in about 2017; the Military Prosecution dropped most of its objection on 15 December 2021; the Military Court of Appeals decided on 31 March 2022 under a gag order, which was eased on 17 May and lifted on 31 May 2022; the transcripts were published at the end of July 2022 (Akevot; The New Arab; Peoples Dispatch).

Apologies and their wording: President Peres in December 2007, 'A most difficult incident happened here, which we deeply regret' (Ynet's rendering); President Rivlin, the first sitting president to attend the ceremony, on 26 October 2014: 'It was an atrocious massacre. A severe crime was perpetrated here'; President Herzog on 29 October 2021: 'on behalf of myself and the State of Israel, I ask for forgiveness.'

The Knesset voted down a Joint List bill for state recognition of the massacre the day before Herzog's visit (Times of Israel; 93–12 on 26 October 2021 per Wikipedia, citing Haaretz). At the 60th anniversary in 2016 about 4,000 people marched, and Ayman Odeh called on the government to recognize 'the terrible massacre in Kfar Kassem and the historical crimes'.

disputes.question: Was Kafr Qasim part of a plan to expel the Triangle's Arab citizens?

positions.view: Yes, or at least linked: the 2022 transcripts (Levy's testimony on Shadmi's 'desirable' fatalities and 'movement eastward'), Segev's 'contingency plan to expel the inhabitants to Jordan', and PalQuest's account of Plan Mole as intended to terrorize and deport.

Not shown by the released record: the plan's own text stays redacted, Shadmi denied the order covered returning workers, two of three units did not shoot, and the 1958 court tried the killing as an unlawful order by named officers, not as a state plan; the documents establish testimony about intent, not an executed policy.

claims.text: The United States voted for the UN resolutions condemning the invasion and 'approving the creation of a U.N. peacekeeping force', and 'pressured Britain and France to accept a United Nations ceasefire on November 6' (Office of the Historian).

Hahn: Eisenhower secured a UN cease-fire resolution and organized the UN Emergency Force; the belligerents accepted the cease-fire on 6 November under US political and financial pressure, effective 7 November; UNEF troops arrived in Egypt on 15 November.

FRUS vol. XVI names the sequence: deadlock in the Security Council; the convening of the first emergency special session of the General Assembly; the Anglo-French bombardment; creation of the UN Emergency Force (30 October–5 November, documents 439–498); then the Canal Zone assault, 'the threat of Soviet intervention' and acceptance of a cease-fire (5–6 November, documents 499–533); then 'the European oil supply problem and the activation of the Middle East Emergency Committee's plan' and the Anglo-French decision to withdraw (7 November–4 December).

On 7 November 1956 Eisenhower and Eden spoke by telephone at 8:43, 9:55 and 10:27 a.m.; Eisenhower sent Eden and Mollet messages on the Gruenther mission; and on 8 November at 3:15 p.m. the President spoke with Treasury Secretary Humphrey (FRUS document list, documents 535–563).

The same week the United States made a 'strident condemnation of the Soviet intervention in Hungary', and US public criticism of its allies is linked by the Office of the Historian to Eden's resignation in January 1957.

On 7 November Hammarskjöld told Ambassador Lodge that General Burns reported Israel intended, and might have begun, to force UN Truce Supervision observers out of Gaza, and warned that persistent Israeli defiance could prompt so strong a UN reaction that Israel might be expelled.
Britain and France completed their withdrawal from Port Said on 22 December 1956 (Keightley: last troops aboard at 17:10 GMT).
By March 1957 the US–UK relationship had recovered under Harold Macmillan (Office of the Historian).

An East German paper reported on 6 November from Cairo that British paratroopers had taken the Port Said airfield and called the invasion fleet 'the largest fleet to operate in the Mediterranean since the Allied landing in Sicily', relaying Egyptian claims of civilian casualties without verification.

disputes.question: Why did Eisenhower turn on his allies?

positions.view: The Office of the Historian and Hahn: Washington had not been told of the collusion, feared the Soviets 'would intervene to assist Nasser', and was condemning the Soviet intervention in Hungary the same week.

The money lever: FRUS places the oil supply problem and the Treasury (Humphrey) at the centre of the November decisions, so the cease-fire was enforced as much by financial pressure as by principle (Hahn's 'political and financial pressure'). The sterling details were not verified for this stage.

claims.text: Soviet leaders threatened to 'intervene in the fighting' and to retaliate against London and Paris with weapons of mass destruction; intelligence reports of Soviet forces concentrating in Syria alarmed US officials (Hahn).
The Office of the Historian records US concern about 'the possibility that the Soviets would intervene to assist Nasser' and the US condemnation of the Soviet intervention in Hungary the same week.
Hahn: unrest in Hungary had distracted US officials before the war, and the turmoil left Soviet leaders 'prone to impulsive behavior' in their view.
FRUS titles the 5–6 November documents 'Anglo-French Assault On the Canal Zone; the Threat of Soviet Intervention; Acceptance of a Cease-Fire'.

Bulganin wrote to Ben-Gurion on 5 November 1956; Ben-Gurion replied on 8 November; Bulganin's second note of 15 November referred back to 'my letter to you of 5 November' and demanded Israeli withdrawal, compensation to Egypt and return of property.

Ben-Gurion's reply of 17 November: 'It was, therefore, the elementary duty of our Government to take defensive measures'; 'Any return to the Armistice Agreement means a return to murder, blockade, and boycott, directed against Israel'; and 'We have not destroyed a single Egyptian town, nor have we caused harm to any civilian centre.'

Eisenhower to King Saud, 16 November 1956: he cited 'the ruthless suppression of the people of Hungary in their quest for freedom' as 'indicative of the fate of any who become dominated by the Soviet Union' and asked the King to encourage Egypt to cooperate on 'the fundamental problems which gave rise to the current crisis'; Saud's own message had spoken of 'Israeli-French-U.K. aggression against Egypt'.

On 8 November Assistant Secretary Rountree told Eban that Israel's withdrawal mattered for 'Western-Soviet relations and the relationship between the United States and Israel', and that failing to comply 'would endanger world peace'.

Bulganin to Ben-Gurion, 5 November 1956: the Israeli government 'is playing with the fate of peace, with the fate of its own people, in a criminal and irresponsible manner', a policy that 'will place a question [mark] upon the very existence of Israel as a State'; the Soviet government had decided to advise its ambassador 'to leave Israel and immediately go to Moscow'.

Ben-Gurion's reply of 8 November expressed 'surprise and sorrow at the threat against Israel's existence and well-being contained in your Note' and said Israel's course 'is not and will not be decided by any foreign factor'.

Bulganin's letter to Mollet of the same day (Documents diplomatiques français) said, in CVCE's summary, that the USSR was prepared to employ 'all modern forms of destructive weaponry' to halt the intervention in Egypt.

JTA (23 November 1956) reported that the letters to Eden, Mollet and Ben-Gurion demanded immediate withdrawal and reparations to Egypt and objected to stationing the UN force anywhere but on both sides of the armistice lines.

disputes.question: Did the Soviet threat or American pressure force the cease-fire and Israel's 8 November retreat?

positions.view: The Soviet threat: Moscow's nuclear-tinged warnings and reports from Syria made the war look like a path to great-power escalation, and Israeli accounts give the Bulganin letter weight.

American pressure: the Office of the Historian and Hahn credit US 'political and financial pressure' and the UN votes; Washington also treated the Soviet threat as a reason to end the war quickly rather than as the cause of the end.

claims.text: At a ceremony at Sharm el-Sheikh the day after the fighting ended (about 6 November), Dayan read a letter from Ben-Gurion to the troops linking the conquest to biblical history and saying that Yotvat (Tiran), described as a former independent Hebrew state, 'will return to be part of the Third Kingdom of Israel' (Walla, 2023, quoting the Hebrew).

Uri Avnery, a journalist at the time, recalled Ben-Gurion's 'victory announcement ... proclaiming the "Third Kingdom of Israel"' and, within about a day, 'his speech announcing, in a broken voice, that he had acceded to President Eisenhower's request and agreed to the retreat.' (Recollection by a political opponent.)

In the Knesset on 7 November Ben-Gurion declared that 'The armistice agreement with Egypt is dead and buried and cannot be restored to life', that the armistice lines had 'no more validity', and that 'On no account will Israel agree to the stationing of a foreign force, no matter how it is called, in its territory' or in any area held by Israel; he also offered direct peace talks with Egypt without preconditions.

Eisenhower's message of 7 November (sent 6:52 p.m. Washington time; a copy handed to Reuven Shiloah at 6:15) warned that an Israeli refusal to withdraw 'could not but bring about the condemnation of Israel as a violator' and could 'impair the friendly cooperation between our two countries', and urged Ben-Gurion to 'comply with the resolutions of the United Nations General Assembly'; as of 2 a.m. it had not yet reached him.

Ben-Gurion's reply of 8 November: Israel would 'willingly withdraw our forces' upon 'conclusion of satisfactory arrangements with the United Nations' for the international force; 'We have never planned to annex the Sinai desert'; and Egypt should abandon 'its policy of boycott and blockade' and enter direct peace negotiations.

The Israeli government's statement of 8 November said 'It was finally agreed to accept the United Nations Resolution and withdraw Israel's forces', listed three aims (destroying the forces that threatened Israel, liberating Israeli territory held by an invader, and free navigation in the Gulf of Eilat and the Canal), of which only the first had been fully achieved, and quoted the Prime Minister: 'There is no power in the world which can nullify our victory.'

On 8 November Eban told Rountree that the manner of withdrawal mattered as much as the act; the State Department opposed a Ben-Gurion visit to Washington that would bypass the UN and approved a meeting only 'after compliance'.

Uri Bar-Joseph (H-Diplo) summarizes the episode as 'brutal pressures' by the Eisenhower administration leading Ben-Gurion to announce a full withdrawal 24 hours after a Knesset speech implying Israel was not ready for one, a memory that weighed on Israel's cabinet in June 1967.

On 16 November Begin praised the government's refusal to leave Sinai until Egypt made peace and, in the Begin Center's summary, concluded that parts of the Land of Israel still needed to be liberated.

disputes.question: What did the 'Third Kingdom' rhetoric mean?

positions.view: A territorial and messianic claim, quickly abandoned: Ben-Gurion's letter and his Knesset tone tied Tiran and Sinai to biblical kingdoms (Walla; Avnery).
Rhetoric, not policy: the 8 November reply states Israel 'never planned to annex the Sinai desert' and the cabinet accepted withdrawal within a day; the operative aims were security and navigation.

claims.text: UNRWA's Special Report of the Director covering 1 November to mid-December 1956 (A/3212/Add.1, GAOR 11th session, Suppl. 14A) records that 'The town of Khan Yunis and the Agency's camp adjacent thereto were occupied by Israel troops on the morning of 3 November' (para. 23).
Khan Yunis: the Director received lists 'numbering 275 Individuals, of whom 140 were refugees and 135 local residents of Khan Yunis'; 'The exact number of dead and wounded is not known' (para. 23).

Both accounts as the report gives them: the Israeli authorities 'state that there was resistance to their occupation and that the Palestinian refugees formed part of the resistance'; the refugees state 'that all resistance had ceased at the time' and that 'many unarmed civilians were killed as the Israel troops went through the town and camp'; the Director notes 'some conflict in the accounts given as to the causes of the casualties' (para. 23).

Rafah, 12 November: the incident 'occurred during a screening operation conducted by the Israel forces'; Israel said the refugees were 'hostile' and there was 'some resistance', which the refugees deny; the Director's finding: loudspeaker announcements 'were not heard by some of the refugee population' and 'some Israel soldiers apparently panicked and opened fire on this running crowd'; the lists numbered '111, of whom 103 were refugees, seven local residents, and one an Egyptian' (paras. 24–27).

Limits stated by the Director: UN Truce Supervision officers could not investigate because their movement in Gaza 'had been restricted by the Israel authorities'; 'It has not been possible to verify individually listed death[s]'; 'it is most unlikely that lists of casualties can ever be made complete', as many burials 'were made without identification' (paras. 21, 30).

Beyond the two incidents, the Director received a list of 'sixty-six individuals, of whom forty-eight were refugees', killed in smaller incidents from 1 to 21 November, some in fighting, some for curfew breaches, some accidentally; he called Khan Yunis and Rafah 'the only major ones of their kind' (para. 29).

Benny Morris: at Khan Yunis, 'some 275 civilians and POWs were murdered' according to the Palestinians and UNRWA; at Rafah Israel said 48 were killed, UNRWA 111; dozens more, mostly captured fedayeen or Egyptian POWs, were killed in the following weeks. Morris sets this against the fedayeen raids run by Egyptian military intelligence in 1954–56.

Other figures reported, each attributed: Palestinian sources 415 killed at Khan Yunis plus 57 missing; Abdel Aziz al-Rantisi (via Filiu) 525 Gazans killed; local residents to Joe Sacco about 100 shot at the Khan Yunis caravanserai; for Rafah a Palestinian figure of 197 killed and 23 disappeared and a Times (London) report of 'some 60'; Morris in 1994/2011 'about two hundred' across both towns (all via Wikipedia's articles, reference only).

TIME (on Sacco's Footnotes in Gaza): 'Israel denies that either event was a massacre', disputes the figures and says its soldiers killed smaller numbers while suppressing riots and resistance; Sacco reconstructed both from survivors' testimony he calls subject to 'the frailty of memory'.

Amira Hass (2010) reports the UN estimates as 275 at Khan Yunis and more than 100 at Rafah, notes no photographs of the killings appear to exist, and treats a witness who was six in 1956 with explicit caution.

disputes.question: What happened at Khan Yunis and Rafah, and how many died?

positions.view: Massacre of civilians: refugees told UNRWA resistance had ended; Palestinian counts run from 275 to 415 (plus missing) at Khan Yunis and 197 at Rafah; Sacco's witnesses describe men lined up and shot.

Israel's account: troops met armed resistance at Khan Yunis and a riot at Rafah; Israel put Rafah's dead at 48 and denies a massacre. The UN Director could verify neither version and judged Rafah a panic by some soldiers; Morris, an Israeli historian, accepts the term massacre for both.

claims.text: Israel's military government ruled 'some 300,000 Palestinian Arabs', about three-quarters of them 1948 refugees (Morris).

Under occupation a curfew was imposed and from 5 November lifted for six daytime hours; by late November there was 'generally free movement of persons throughout the Strip outside curfew hours'; screening continued 'apparently in an orderly fashion' with detainees taken to interrogation centres; refugees lived 'under considerable tension' (UNRWA report).

UNRWA warned that 'unless immediate measures were taken to put an end to such happenings' it could not continue its work, and put staff with no work on leave without pay after 1 January 1957 (paras. 17, 28).

Morris: municipal councils were reinstated (Khan Yunis's on 3 December 1956); schools reopened with 30 of 200 textbooks removed as Egyptian propaganda; by late December four police stations staffed by locals operated under Israel Police supervision; Bedouin in the coastal dunes were ordered to move south-west of Rafah (UN envoy Col. K. R. Nelson's report of 16 December); monuments to Col. Mustafa Hafiz, who had run the fedayeen, were destroyed.

Ben-Gurion hoped to keep Gaza and eastern Sinai: on 19 December 1956 he told the Knesset Israel would never let Egypt resume control of the Strip, and on 23 January 1957 argued 'This Strip was never Egyptian'; a government 'Blueprint for Gaza' (31 January 1957) called Gaza and nearby Jewish settlements 'a topographical and economic unit' (Morris).

The Gush Katif Heritage Center records a Nahal outpost at Rafiah on 3 January 1957, a government resolution of 13 January 1957 that 'Israel will hold the Gaza Strip' and opposing a UN force for its security, and Knesset approval on 23 January 1957 of the decision not to withdraw from Gaza.

In January 1957 Israel agreed to pull its army out of Gaza while leaving police and administrative forces, then withdrew in stages; it left Gaza completely on 8 March 1957 (Walla); Morris also dates the withdrawal to 8 March 1957, 'under international (mainly US) pressure', after four months of military rule.
Egypt had never given Gaza's inhabitants Egyptian citizenship (Morris); the Egyptian administration of 1948–56 is told in rd6 (egi_src_s02).

disputes.question: Did Israel mean to keep Gaza?

positions.view: Yes: Ben-Gurion's December and January Knesset statements, the 13 January cabinet resolution, the Knesset vote of 23 January, the Blueprint and the Nahal outpost all point to retention.

Security, not annexation, was the stated reason: Israel argued only it could stop fedayeen raids from the Strip and asked for UN, not Egyptian, administration as its condition for leaving (Walla; Ben-Gurion, March 1957).

claims.text: On 15 February 1957 the US embassy reported Ben-Gurion 'pleased with intent of United States suggestions if not their particulars' on Tiran but fearing UNEF might leave Sharm el-Sheikh before a settlement, in which case Israel would have 'no other recourse than to fight or submit'; on Gaza 'Prospect which he most adamantly opposes is return of Egyptian authority there under any guise'; 'He frankly hoping for time'.

Around 18–19 February Ben-Gurion appealed to Dulles 'personally to obtain postponement of UN discussions', warning that 'withdrawal under present circumstances will spell disaster for us' and that for the UN to proceed 'is to adopt double standard of morality'; he recalled Eban for consultation.

About 22 February Ben-Gurion said Israel was prepared to withdraw its military forces from Gaza and would not occupy Sharm el-Sheikh 'after Israel's free passage through Tiran Straits had been assured', that Eban would make 'further effort to reach understanding with USG', and that against sanctions 'we shall resist it with every ounce of our moral strength'.

Ben-Gurion's account (5 March 1957) of the US memorandum of 11 February: it 'declares that the United States is ready to make use of freedom of passage in the Straits' and welcomed a UN force at Sharm el-Sheikh; he quotes Eisenhower's 20 February address that 'we should not assume that if Israel withdraws, Egypt will prevent Israeli shipping', and says a letter from Eisenhower of 2 March preceded the cabinet's approval of withdrawal from Gaza on 2 March.

On 1 March 1957 the government authorized the Foreign Minister (Golda Meir) to announce at the UN that 'Israel will withdraw from the Gaza Strip and Sharm el-Sheikh', on the stated assumption 'That the take-over from the military and civilian control of Israel will be exclusively by the UNEF', and declared that interference with Israeli ships 'will be regarded by Israel as an attack entitling it' to act in self-defence.

Israel completed its withdrawal from Gaza on 8 March 1957 and from Sinai the same month; UNEF remained in Egypt 'as a buffer against Egyptian-Israeli hostilities' until Nasser ordered it out in May 1967.

What Israel claimed it gained: free passage through Tiran ('vital to Israel, and is also of great importance to other countries') and UN forces at Sharm el-Sheikh and in Gaza (Ben-Gurion, 5 March 1957). The government had said on 8 November 1956 that only the first of its three war aims had then been fully achieved.

disputes.question: Did Israel withdraw with guarantees or without them?

positions.view: With assurances: the 11 February US memorandum on the Straits, Eisenhower's 20 February words and his 2 March letter, and UNEF at Sharm el-Sheikh gave Israel what Ben-Gurion called the campaign's gains.

Without formal guarantees: Israel left 'without formal security gains' under 'brutal' US pressure (Bar-Joseph); the assurances were unilateral statements and assumptions, and UNEF could be (and in 1967 was) withdrawn at Egypt's request.

claims.text: Eden resigned in January 1957; the Office of the Historian links his fall to US public criticism of the allies; by March 1957 US–UK relations had recovered under Macmillan.

The Eisenhower Doctrine of early 1957 pledged economic and military aid and, if necessary, force to contain communism in the Middle East; under it the United States 'immediately dispensed tens of millions of dollars in aid' to Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Lebanon and Libya (Hahn). Israel is not on Hahn's list.
The Office of the Historian presents the Doctrine as a response to US concerns about European power in the region that 'gave the administration increased power to aid countries in the region'.
Nasser gained prestige among Arab peoples as 'a leader who had defied European empires and survived a military invasion by Israel' (Hahn).

The Jewish Agency's account notes that many Egyptian Jews emigrated to Israel as 'an indirect outcome of the war'; the November 1956 expulsions and the 23 November proclamation are documented in rd6's research (jews_arab_world_1948_1956).

Oren (interpretation): Israel emerged 'economically, diplomatically, and militarily stronger', and the war partly fulfilled goals left open by the 1949 armistices; he reports that Shlaim and other New Historians argued Israel paid a heavy political price for aligning with colonial powers, and that Fromkin called the victory Pyrrhic.
Ben-Gurion himself warned the IDF command on 27 December 1956 that the next war 'could be a prolonged one' and that Israel might be 'the defenders' rather than the attackers.

The Knesset that fought the war also saw, on 29 October 1957, the first anniversary of the campaign and of Kafr Qasim, a grenade thrown into the plenum that wounded Ben-Gurion and several ministers (JVL Knesset highlights).

positions.view: Israel did, militarily and strategically: Tiran opened, the fedayeen stopped, the French alliance (and reactor) secured (Oren); the IDF calls it 'an impressive military success' because it halted attacks from the Egyptian border.

Nasser did, politically: he kept the Canal and won Arab prestige, while Britain and France lost their regional role and Israel was tied to colonial powers and forced out without a treaty (Hahn; Shlaim and Fromkin as reported by Oren).

claims.text: In the Security Council, Britain and France vetoed both the US draft (S/3710) and the Soviet draft (S/3713/Rev.1), each of which called for Israel to withdraw (UN University's Uniting for Peace case study; the Council's own Resolution 119 cites the 'lack of unanimity' at its 749th and 750th meetings of 30 October).

Resolution 119 (31 October 1956, S/3721), adopted at the 751st meeting by 7 votes to 2 (France and the United Kingdom against; Australia and Belgium abstaining), called an emergency special session of the General Assembly under the Uniting for Peace procedure, 'Considering that a grave situation has been created by action undertaken against Egypt'.

The first emergency special session convened at 5 p.m. on 1 November 1956 and adopted Resolution 997 (ES-I), from the US draft (A/3256), at about 4:20 a.m. on 2 November after some five hours of debate (FRUS editorial note).

Resolution 997 urged an immediate cease-fire and a halt to moving forces and arms into the area; urged the armistice parties to withdraw behind the armistice lines, stop raids and observe the 1949 agreements; recommended that members not send military goods to the area; urged that the Suez Canal be reopened once the cease-fire took effect; asked the Secretary-General to report on compliance; and kept the Assembly in emergency session.

The vote on 997: 64 in favour, 5 against (Australia, France, Israel, New Zealand, United Kingdom), 6 abstentions (Belgium, Canada, Laos, Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa). Canada abstained because the text had no UN step toward a settlement; Pearson wanted the Secretary-General authorized to arrange a UN force, and Dulles said the US would welcome a Canadian proposal.

Resolution 998 (ES-I), 4 November 1956: 57 in favour, none against, 19 abstentions (including Britain, France, Israel, Egypt, the Soviet Union and its allies). Resolution 999, same day: 59–5–12 (the same five against). Resolution 1000, 5 November: 57–0–19. (Roll calls from the UN Project; the texts of 998, 999 and 1000, which created and organized UNEF, were not fetched.)

Resolutions 1001 and 1002 (ES-I) were adopted at the 567th plenary on 7 November 1956 (A/3354). Resolution 1002 'Calls once again upon Israel immediately to withdraw all its forces behind the armistice lines' of the 24 February 1949 agreement and calls 'once again upon the United Kingdom and France immediately to withdraw all their forces from Egyptian territory'; the Jewish Virtual Library gives its vote as 65–1–10.

Resolution 1124 (XI), 2 February 1957, adopted 74–2–2: it 'Deplores the non-compliance of Israel to complete its withdrawal behind the armistice demarcation line' and calls on Israel to complete it 'without further delay'; it follows Resolution 1123 of 19 January 1957.

disputes.question: Was the UN's line against the invasion a US-led consensus or a broad one?

positions.view: US-led: 997 was the US draft and the US carried the Assembly against its own allies (FRUS; Office of the Historian).

Broad but not universal: only the three invaders plus Australia and New Zealand voted no; Canada and several Western states abstained on 997 for wanting a UN force rather than a bare cease-fire, and the Soviet bloc abstained on the UNEF resolutions.

claims.text: The US aide-mémoire handed to Eban on 11 February 1957 (released 17 February) said Israeli withdrawal from Gaza 'should be prompt and unconditional', that UNEF should 'move into this area and be on the boundary between Israel and the Gaza Strip', that 'the gulf comprehends international waters' where no nation may prevent 'free and innocent passage', and that the US 'is prepared to exercise the right of free and innocent passage and to join with others' to secure it.

Meeting Robert Murphy on 11 February, Eban said that if nothing else Israel had 'focused American thinking on the Gulf of Aqaba problem', and that 'a good deal of the momentum in favor of sanctions would evaporate' once the American position was known.

At the bipartisan meeting at the White House on 20 February (8:30–10:55 p.m.), Eisenhower said sanctions 'might take various forms'; Dulles listed 'German reparation payments to Israel, world-wide sale of Israeli government bonds, and US aid' as areas for consideration. Knowland proposed a resolution under which failure to comply in 30 days 'would properly subject the offender to economic, moral and diplomatic sanctions'; Lyndon Johnson 'asked if sanctions were the best move'; Fulbright wanted nothing that looked like 'a commitment to go to war'; Rayburn wanted no 'part of a Congressional resolution'.

Dulles to Senator Johnson (delivered 22 February, replying to Johnson's letter of 11 February): 'There is strong sentiment among many members of the United Nations for economic sanctions'; the President would be 'reluctant' to see sanctions become the only remedy; Israel had received 'important assurances' but 'apparently has felt that those assurances were not sufficient'.

Eisenhower's radio and television address of 20 February 1957 asked: 'Should a nation which attacks and occupies foreign territory in the face of United Nations disapproval be allowed to impose conditions on its own withdrawal?'; said Israel 'insists on firm guarantees as a condition to withdrawing its forces of invasion'; and warned that 'the United Nations has no choice but to exert pressure upon Israel to comply with the withdrawal resolutions'.

The same address said UNEF 'should be placed on the Egyptian-Israeli Armistice lines', that the Gaza Strip should no longer be 'a source of armed infiltration and reprisals', that 'no nation has the right to prevent free and innocent passage in the Gulf', and that the US had given Israel 'on February 11 a statement of United States policy'. It does not mention US aid to Israel.

On 28 February Dulles told the British, Canadian and French envoys that Israel would announce, in effect, 'its unconditional withdrawal in the areas now occupied', getting nothing beyond prior UN resolutions, while stating 'assumptions' already in UN texts and its 'expectations'; the US position on Aqaba was unchanged from the 11 February aide-mémoire.

disputes.question: Did the United States threaten Israel with sanctions?

positions.view: Yes in substance: the President publicly said the UN had 'no choice but to exert pressure', and Dulles named reparations, bonds and US aid as possible levers to congressional leaders.

Not formally: no US sanction was imposed; Dulles told Johnson the President was 'reluctant' to reach sanctions; congressional leaders of both parties resisted; the deal of 1 March came through assurances, not penalties.

claims.text: Eisenhower asked Congress on 5 January 1957 for military and economic aid to Middle Eastern states and authority to use force to protect them, after a four-hour White House meeting with congressional leaders on 1 January (Waxman).
The House passed H.J. Res. 117 on 30 January 1957 by 355–61; the Senate passed it as amended on 5 March 1957 by 72–19 (Voteview roll calls).

Public Law 85-7 (71 Stat. 5), approved 9 March 1957, section 1: the President is 'authorized to cooperate with and assist any nation or group of nations in the general area of the Middle East' in developing economic strength to maintain independence.

Section 2: the United States 'is prepared to use armed forces' if the President deems it necessary to assist any requesting nation 'against armed aggression from any country controlled by international communism', 'consonant with the treaty obligations of the United States and with the Constitution'.

Section 3: up to $200,000,000 'from any appropriation now available' under the Mutual Security Act of 1954 for the rest of fiscal 1957, usable only 15 days after a report to the committees; the resolution itself authorized no new appropriation. Section 4 supported UNEF; section 5 required reports each January and July; section 6 let it expire on a presidential finding or a concurrent resolution.

Senator Richard Russell warned against any appearance that only 'a small war' might follow; Eisenhower replied that 'should Russia move it could not possibly be a small war'; in 1958 Eisenhower sent about 14,000 troops to Lebanon without citing the resolution (Waxman).

disputes.question: Was the Doctrine about communism or about replacing Britain and France?

positions.view: Communism, by its text: the force clause is limited to aggression 'from any country controlled by international communism'.

Replacing the old powers: the Office of the Historian presents it as a response to US concern about European power in the region after Suez, and Hahn records the aid flowing at once to regional allies.

claims.text: The Anglo-French offensive 'greatly accelerated the drain on U.K. reserves'; a 'massive loss of reserves' in November pushed them below the Bank of England's $2 billion floor for defending the $2.80 parity (Boughton, IMF).

Treasury Secretary Humphrey's position was that the US would support Britain when it was 'conforming to rather than defying the United Nations'; Macmillan's attempt to meet him in late November failed (Boughton).

On 3 December Humphrey proposed an immediate drawing of $561 million plus a stand-by of about $739 million, $1.3 billion in all (100% of the UK quota); Macmillan announced the November losses and 'an immediate approach' to the IMF on 4 December; the Board approved with one abstention (Egypt), and the UK drew $561 million at once.
All four combatants obtained IMF financing, 'highly unusual for the time' (Boughton's working paper).

European oil supplies had fallen '25 to 30 percent below their normal needs' by mid-November (a British and French claim), and until the end of November the US refused to activate 'the plan of action prepared by the Middle East Emergency Committee', offering oil 'if those two countries complied with the United Nations resolutions' and withdrew (FRUS editorial note).

On 25 November Eisenhower explained the delay: 'we have held up this measure until the invading powers accepted immediate withdrawal of their troops'; Hoover urged starting the emergency committee 'very soon', and the President wanted it announced as preventing 'widespread suffering in Europe'.

positions.view: Yes: the reserve drain and Humphrey's condition tied British financing to compliance with the UN, and oil was held back until withdrawal was accepted (Boughton; FRUS).

Part of a wider pressure: the UN votes, the Soviet threats and Britain's own cabinet decision of 6 November came first; the IMF package followed the cease-fire and the withdrawal decision rather than preceding them.

entries.topic: The Jews of Egypt, November 1956–1958: arrests, the nationality law, sequestration and departure

sources.label: Brenda Gazzar, JTA, 21 December 2006 (Ramat Gan, 18 December), on the 1956 expulsions from Egypt
Lyn Julius, "The Suez Crisis and the Jews of Egypt", Fathom (Autumn 2017) (author directs the advocacy group Harif)

claims.text: About 1,000 Jews in Egypt, many of them Egyptian citizens, were detained or imprisoned during the Suez crisis; about 500 Jews without British or French passports were expelled alongside the many Jews among the expelled British and French nationals (JTA, 2006, citing historians).

Julius records a first wave of about 500 Jews given 24 hours to leave, about 900 more arrested by 7 November 1956, and detention at the Abbasiya school (500, half stateless) and Les Barrages prison (300).

Nationality Law No. 391 of 1956 (22 November 1956) barred 'Zionists', a term it never defined, from Egyptian nationality and let the Interior Ministry declare nationality forfeited (Article 18) (JJAC report, advocacy, crediting the Historical Society of Jews from Egypt).
On 23 November 1956 a proclamation by the Minister of Religious Affairs, read in mosques, declared that 'all Jews are Zionists and enemies of the state' and promised their expulsion (Julius; JJAC).

Sequestration under Military Proclamation No. 4: orders of 1–20 November 1956 placed hundreds of Jews' property under Egyptian administrators, with published lists of 486 persons and firms at least 95% Jewish (JJAC); about 500 Jewish companies were sequestered from November 1956 to March 1957 (JTA 2006; Julius), with about 800 more enterprises blacklisted and a 10% custodian fee (Julius).
Departing Jews received exit visas stamped 'ONE WAY-NO RETURN', signed declarations 'donating' property to the state, and could take one suitcase and a small sum (Julius).

Between 23,000 and 25,000 Jews left Egypt from November 1956 through 1957 (JTA) or 1958 (Julius), by expulsion or heavy pressure; more than 6,000 left by ship with the Red Cross by 1957; the community was about 15,000 by 1957 (JJAC); roughly half of Egypt's Jews eventually went to Israel (Julius).

Julius also records the limits: Egyptian-national Jews were initially spared, some expulsion orders were rescinded, Greeks, Armenians and Italians were not targeted in 1956, and the wider nationalizations of the 1960s also hit non-Jewish families.

disputes.question: Why were Egypt's Jews forced out in 1956–57?

positions.view: State persecution of Jews as Jews: the 23 November proclamation, the 'Zionist' nationality clause and sequestration lists over 95% Jewish (Julius; JJAC; Krämer, as Julius reports her, that Jews alone were targeted because of the conflict).

Decolonization and war measures against enemy nationals, sharpened by Israel's war and Operation Susannah: Julius reports Joel Beinin's view blaming Zionism and notes that British and French nationals were expelled too; Mendes (rd6) finds many left for economic reasons.
